blocks.x: I have to go to work at 10. When you were 10, yeah. Yeah, and she had three children younger than me. Is it starting now?
Yes, it's going all right. If you want to give your age first.
I want to give my age a name first.
Yes, if you want to give your name now.
I want to do that first.

Good, all right. And you won't have to lean forward because you can just, this will pick up or it will pick you up even outdoors. So you don't have to lean forward, just relax and sit back and it will pick up anything in the room. So you can give your name now if you would.

Thanks. My name is William Ridgely. I was born in Jefferson Parish, January 15, 18 and 82. My mother died when I was 10 and I had to go to work. And there was some German people that I knew that ran a country grocery about two city blocks from where I was born. And they gave me a job. And I worked for those people about 18 years. And after I was with them a while, it was a place where most of the men in the country gathered in the evening and sat around and talked. And a lot of young boys. And I used to do a lot of entertaining at night with those men by dancing and singing. Some of the boys played banjo. And we made up in our mind to set up what we call a string band. There were six of us. And I was in the points. And so my people that I worked for, they bought a bass violin for me. That was the first instrument that I started on. And there were six of us. We didn't have any trombone player at that time.
What were the instruments in that family?
There was bass violin, banjo, clarinet, cornet, and drums.
I see. And what were you playing?
I played bass violin. And Professor Umphrey, James Umphrey, was our instructor. And he lived in New Orleans. We lived in the parish.
Just about where was that in the Jefferson?

About one mile and a quarter out of the city limit. And we used to have to meet Professor Umphrey every Sunday morning about 9 o'clock. We had a little road cart. We'd carry him, flurry and two. And so the people that I wait for, they give us a place that we could have our practice, take our lessons, and might near every night while we was there playing and doing the best that we could. And so Professor Umphrey, I had to take him back in for it. And he advised me to buy a trombone. And I agreed to do so. And he bought me a trombone, paid eight dollars for it, a silver bell, a method, and a catechism. So I would take bass violins on Sunday. And during the week one day, I would come to his house on Liberty Street in New Orleans with my trombone. He told me that it wasn't much, no difference in the music much. Just you had to learn the precessions and learn how to blow. And I thought that was very good. And a little while after that, this band broke up. And probably about two months later, there was an old man by the name of Lambert, Henry Lambert. He was an old musician, old tuba player. And he organized this bunch again. And he played the vowel trombone this time in the band. And we had another professor then by the name of Frank Welch, one of the old coinette players, and his son was the drummer. So then he played. We had two coinettes then in the band. And he taught us and played coinette along with us. And later, this band broke up. And Professor Welch then, he brought us to New Orleans and joined us in with the Silver Leaf Band under the leadership then of Albert Batiste. And our first playing...
Do you remember about, excuse me, what year that was about? Was that...

That could have been about 1910. 1910, when you joined the Silver Leaf. Silver Leaf Band. I was still living in Jefferson Paris. And then I moved to New Orleans in 1911. And I was still with Silver Leaf Band. And Mr. Welch, he was a sickly man and he gave up the coinette playing. And we got over to the fellow by the name of Hippolyte Charles. He played coinette for us a while. And then he gave up the coinette playing and old man Welch came back again. And old man Welch made me to know Celestine. He said he was a very fine fellow and he think would make a good coinette player. And that we would try to use him. So we got acquainted with Celestine and he got us with us. And he played along in Silver Leaf Band with me. And then later he got a job playing in the old district at the 101 Ranch. And him and I went in the district to play together. And we joined in with another bunch of fellows. And when the old district closed, then him and I organized the Tuxedo Band. He was playing there but I never did. And we joined the Tuxedo Band and we got another bunch of fellows. Around 1914 we were still in the old district. And I think then it came to close again. And we got our band out in the field. We call it the Tuxedo Jazz Band. Celestine, myself, Johnny Lindsay, Ernest Trapani, Lorenzo Teo, Peter... Who was the river? Peter Bocard. Peter Bocard. And that was our boy stand. And from that we went on and doing pretty good. And something happened that some of those men left. But Celestine and I still was together. And then I got me a band headquarters on Howard Avenue between Drys and Barone. And run the Preston Shop and the Shoe Black stand. And that was our headquarters. And from that on we began to grow faster. And getting in much work, I got to know a white gentleman by the name of Sim Black. He was scoutmaster of Boy Scout Troop Thirteen. And he used to visit our band quarters pretty regularly. So one day he came in and he said originally, he said, I have a suggestion for you. He said, something I think will improve the band. And he said, I was thinking that if you all would get black tuxedo suit, derby hat, white shirts, said, and I think it would help the band a great deal. And that was just about the time for the deputy season to open. And that time, the late Henry Zeno was playing drums for me. And he taken up on him to go out to find a tuxedo suit. We find him at the mass, that ain't right. Is there a tailor shop you found them? Yes, tailor shop. And it cost us $15 a piece. And from then on, our band just went on like a blaze of fire. And we used to play during the wartime. Played at Heinemann Park every Sunday for the baseball season. We played every year on the 6th of January for the 12th Night Revlon at the Arthenaire. We played all of the great ball, mostly for all of the carnival clubs. And we were well thought of by the people. And in 1923, we went to Fort Worth with the Pelicans on the southern season with the police band of New Orleans. And some ladies from Texas know that our band were coming and asked us what would we charge them to play a half an hour. They were raising a $25,000 milk fund. And we agreed to play for them for nothing. They treated us good, taking us all over Fort Worth. And police band was very nice to us. And on our way back in New Orleans, then we played in the largest chair in the world that had been all around the world. Taking the bass, violin, drums, and the whole band put it up on a truck. Now the tuxedo band, we called it the Tuxedo Jazz Band. But Mr. Sim Black suggested that we would call the band the original Tuxedo Band. And that's who named the band at that time.
You had already called it the Tuxedo Band though before you started the tuxedos. Is that right? Yes. And he was a big help to us.

And during his vacation with his troop, Boy Scouts 13, we went down to Kentwood and we spent one day in the swamps with them. And when we came back to New Orleans, we played a dance at each of those boys' house. And that was the life of the Tuxedo Band at that time. It was well thought of. Played New Orleans Country Club, Southern Yacht Country Club, and other, all the places, all the hotels. Roosevelt, St. Charles, Louisiana, all places. Most every place that was in the city of New Orleans and outstate of Louisiana, we played almost everywhere at a colored band, could go. Never had any trouble. Everybody treated us all right. I'm tired now.
Do you want to rest a minute? Yes. Okay, we have to turn it off for a second. So we have it going again. Did you want to tell who was in the Tuxedo Band when they went to Fort Worth?
How do you say that?
If you want to give the list of the musicians again. Paul Barnes, you say you forgot to mention him.
You want to name our band?
Yes, yes, name.
That went to Fort Worth. Paul Barnes, saxophone. Chinese, drummer. John Marrero, banjo. Simon Marrero, bass. Celestine, cornet. William Ridgely, trombone. Emma Barrett, saxophone. Piano.
Piano.

Piano. Piano. And our band, Celestine, was leader. William Ridgely was a bookie agent and businessman. And we went a real good long ways like that until the climax came in 25. That's when the original Tuxedo Band split. Then we had two bands.
Oh yes, I heard about that. Did you take over the original band then?

The original Tuxedo Band and Celestine Tuxedo Band. And we both went big for a while, for about six years. And then after that, I gave up playing all together. And joined the Methodist Church. I've been there ever since. The class leader in the church. Church on the...
Where is your church? Which one?
St. Peter, ME Church, number two, on Eagle Street. And I'm at 3424. Our present pastor is Reverend Tillman Thompson. I became trustee. Now I'm serving on the stored board. And I like it very much.
What kind of music do they have? Do they have the choir I know you mentioned? I have a choir.
I have a junior choir and a senior choir. Mm-hm. And there's stuff there. And there's stuff there. And there's stuff there. And there's stuff there. And there's stuff there.
Not a very large congregation, but we're spiritually strong.
Did they use the organ or piano or any other instruments?
Organs, either piano, either one.
Did they ever use any other instruments in the church?
No, no other instruments in the church.
When you were a boy, do you remember the music in the churches when you were a boy? What kind of songs and spirituals they had?
No music, not in our church when I was a boy. They didn't have any choir even.
Not even a choir?

No. People sang, but they were good. Old time hymn made them up their self and so on like that. And I was a Sunday school boy. I attended the Ross Chapel M.E. Center School in Jefferson College. Now I've been working in the church for about 28 years. And I didn't think anything else could stop me. But we want to name the Tuxedo band that Mr. Sim Black named. That was Chinese, no, Henry Zeno on drum. Tom Benton, banjo. Sam Dutre, clarinet. Celestine, cornet. George Foster, bass. William Ridley, trombone. Emma Barrett, piano.

Can you tell me about the first records you made when you made those phonograph records? Who was in the band? There were some that they were made for okay. A Careless Love and the Black and White, let's see, was it the Black Rag or Black and White Rag?
Black Rag, Careless Love, Poirinelli.
There was one called Original Tuxedo Rag.
Original Tuxedo Rag, that's right. That's right. That's the four.
That other tune was what, Poe Nelly?
Hoey Nelly. Hoey Nelly. H-O-Y-E. Hoey Nelly.
I don't think they issued that then. I don't think that came out, did it?
Well, that's one of our main history.
I don't remember that record. I have the other three numbers. I have those. Can you tell me who was in the band then when they made those? Can you remember? Was it?
Manuel Minetti, piano. William Ridgely, Celestine. Johnny Sincer. Tom Benton. Chani on drum. Samuel Memorero on bass violin. John Marrero, guitar.
Do you remember on Careless Love somebody plays a little slide whistle? Who was that? Who did that?
He was Chinese. The drummer. The drummer. He played the whistle. Mazzucca, we called it, I think. And he was the first to blow in the drum. He used to blow in the drum, take it up like that.
Did he sing along with it or just sort of blow? Oh yeah, like that.
When we went to Texas, my mind could the people went wild over and eat the people. So, uh...
I was going to ask some more about that, uh, the Tuxedo Dance Hall. Did you ever play in the Tuxedo Dance Hall in the district? No. Celestine had been there though, had he?
I was playing with Civil League band at that time.
But you didn't play at the Tuxedo Hall? No, at the Tuxedo Hall. I wondered when they named the band, the very first, did they name it after that hall?

That's right. That's when Celestine and I got together and agreed to organize a band. We called it Tuxedo Jazz Band. That was his idea, Celestine. Because he had been playing on it and he said he thought it would be a hit and it was.
But then it was several years later before you began wearing the tuxedos.

Oh Lord, yeah. Before that. But that's when we got into the money when we got the tuxedos. Things like that. We played all the big dances and everybody. We played all the stool dances, Tulane, Loyola. In fact, we played everything that we could.
Here's one other thing I heard once, something about you went up in an airplane.

Did, Friday, June of 1924. Gates, Flying Cycles, used to come from California every summer. We were playing at that time at Francina's Restaurant at Spanish Fort. And Mr. George Gates engaged us to play in the airplane. Let me get that. That was Celestine, William Racely, John Marrero, Simon Marrero, Paul Barnes, and Williton, a fellow by the name of Williton, on drum at that time.
Could you get out the whole band in the plane? No. The plane big enough then? Two of us. Two at a time.

Two at a time. That's when it was, and the most we played then was Marilyn and Naga Rain the Moor. So dry that scene, you know. So Celestine and I went up together. Then the saxophone and banjo went up together. Then the saxophone and banjo and the clarinet went up together. The bass couldn't be. The rinfo piece.
Was that when you had Sam Dutre with you? Did he go and have Peter Firenette to wind up? Right.
Did Sam Dutre play up in the plane? Did he go up and was he in the band then?
No, he wasn't with us, but I'm trying to. Eddie Chiri. Oh yes. Eddie Chiri. He was playing clarinet the saxophone at the time.

I was going to ask about this picture over here that you showed us the other day. With this group with Pierone and Benton and St. Cyr. I have a copy of this picture. But you said they were going to go on the road for some reason.

This was when the district first closed. And Clarence Williams, he was the man he was here then. And we had those pictures made to play on the Orphan Circa. By some means Pierone and Williams didn't agree. And Clarence Williams went off and left us there. But Pierone was the cause. We didn't get this job. We would have been the first colored band. See, you know what I said. That was 40 years ago. See. Alarm for Dixie. Then.
Before the original Dixie Land left here.
Alarm for them.
Do you remember about what year was it? During the First World War or after it or about when? What year that would be? The war started in 1914. That was after the...

The war in Germany started in Europe in 1914. And we got into it about 1917 or so. Or 18. 17, 17. Ended in 18. But we were playing at the 101 Ranch at that time. That was around 1914. But this picture had been made. See. This picture was made before that.
It was made by 1914 then. Before that. Before 1914. It was made.
See. See. That ought to be about 40 years. That ought to be before.
Oh yes. A long time ago. I was going to ask about Tom Benton. Let's see. He has a... He has a mandolin banjo there. What did he usually play? Did he play guitar, banjo, mandolin or what?
Tom Benton played the... Tom Benton played the... Played... And he was a good ragtime piano player.
Watch. I heard he was piano player.
And a... Pretty good singer. A very good bad band man. He was. And there's him and Johnny there together. So he was very good for the Tom Benton.
What was Clarence Williams doing in this group? Did he sing or play piano some time? Well...
He sang some time. He played piano some time. But I guess he's just going to be general booking agent. Whatever you might call it.
For the booking agent. For the group. For the group, really.

Now we are... Peter Ron never was a member of our band. Peter Booker was a member of our band. He played violin. Yeah. But at this time they make this picture. Peter Ron was a member of our band at that time. He never was. Now you're showing the name of your son of the cornet players? Oh yes. What do you mean? Louis Armstrong. Mark Carey. When did you work with Armstrong? Just... never was a member. But he jobbed around with us in Southern Standard Place at times. He was young. He was very young. He hadn't stopped playing in no bands out yet. I think one time I saw a picture taken on one of the river boats where you were playing with Faith Marable. Did you play with him and Armstrong was in that band? Yeah. We were together. The first year that Armstrong played with Faith, we were together. Louis Armstrong, William Ridgely, George Foster, Joe Howard, Baby Dot. John, what's the guy in California now?
St. Sarah in the band, on the band, John?
Yes, St. Sarah. John the saxophonist, but he's in California. This is David John.
Oh, David John, yeah.
He was playing another for him at that time. John Porter playing bass violin. John Porter played... Bass tubo, you know.
He played tubo, I didn't know he was in front of me.

Yeah, he played bass violin before he got on. He was with us when we went to St. Louis on the first year, but I don't remember when I went there. It was pretty good about 18, 19. Well, that's when Louis, we were all together and he got his first start. But, well, he struck with the boat. But I came back to New Orleans and I went to the Southern Standard and the Savoy River Garden. We were working there together.
Did you ever play drums out there?

Yes. Yes. See, after I faced trouble and I couldn't play drum board anymore, so I tried to drum. Somebody told me you played drums. But I didn't like it because I figured I'd get too old. And then I was trying to even play in the orchestra, you know. And from being trombone sitting in the front of me at the time, well, the people didn't believe that was me, you see. You see, we were to play trombone. So I got so I just didn't like it. And I felt like quitting anyhow, you see. Because we had had such a good reputation in Southern Standard and I had to get and done so well and people cared so much about it. And then I'd take on a young bunch of fellas and I couldn't handle them, you know, like with the older bunch. And I just gave up, you see, because they'd go to risk and ruin my reputation. Because I played at some boy in the garden. I had two of them, one kind of played these days, saxophone player. So they would drink and they were very contrary. And they would run the instrument down while playing, you know, see, and to sound bad. So Mr. Sheen, he was a very good man. He had keen ear for music and he knowed too much about it. So he called me and said to me if I didn't get rid of them fellas, I'd lose my child. And they were both very good players too. But after that they were so hard to handle. I said, well, I'd lose my reputation when I had built up for so many years. I didn't, I guess, give it up. Going into the church business. And I think I'm, but an older musician is in my time. I was older than a lot of the men. And I think I'm almost about the oldest one of them living now.
Yes, I believe you are. Willie Umphrey is about your age, I believe, isn't he?
No, no, I'm older than older.
You're older than he is.
Yeah, I'm, now Albert Glenny was there sometimes, he was the one of the kids.
Oh yes, he was old.

He was the one man. But I think now, among that bunch that I came along with, I was older than all of these. I was older than any I ever played. And any of those on the picture you ever played? Oh yeah. I was about to see Peter Volkow. And Peter on too, I guess I was about to see him. I was older than all those men. And I often look at that picture and I said, well sir, I'd be older than all. I think because I stopped playing. I don't think they put on my life.
It might have helped, although some, Albert Glenny kept playing until he was quite old, didn't he? Yeah, exactly. I can put this picture back if you like.
Did you say you, say something about when you changed from bass violin to...
Yes, you traded your bass as on...

We were, I was with several lead bands when I was trading from trombone, bass violin to trombone. See, we had the old man who was a key trombone player, you know. But in the beginning, when he came in the band, but after he was with us a while, he went back to the bass violin, you see, then he took the bass violin and I played trombone because Mr. Wells said that he thought the slight trombone was more exciting among the people and what they would have trombone. And I think so too and we went along pretty good.
It kind of looks more exciting.
Yeah, it was something new, different.
Did you play about the same kind of a part on the slide as they used on the valve? No, you had a little more white cut.

But it wasn't nothing like now, you know, not the slight trombone, nothing now. But it was a little bit different from the valve trombone. But you see at that time it was more sliding, the thing they get was more exciting, you see. But those guys now is cutting them trombone like a cronet player. Oh yeah.
You play mainly bass parts, I guess.
Bass parts, that's right. I think they play mostly the bass parts.

I wondered in the old days when I was a young kid, I remember some of those pieces like Slim Trombone and there were a whole family of different pieces that the Fillmore published. Do you remember some of those? I think Rastus Trombone, Slim Trombone, different names of some of those pieces. Sally Trombone. Sally Trombone. Did you ever play those pieces?

I played Slim Trombone, I think. I never really had a solid trombone. We played sliding jim and various other things we used to make ourselves, you know, at that time. We'd done more sliding than anything else, you see, because that's what made the hit at that time. We played the side somewhere.
We played a sliding jim. Was that a famous thing there?
We hit an in-muted with Marilyn, Furinella, Liza Jane, Downholm Ray. High Society, Tiger Ray, Clarinet Mamalee.
Did you play many blues when you were in the church?
Yes, blues, plenty. All kind of blues. We had all of the blues. Did you usually just make up the blues or did you play? We did. We had a corner player I didn't mention, Lewis Madison Schatz.
Oh yes, I knew him.
He came in after the Sillis and I split. Well he was a very good blues player. He made a hit on most anything he played. He was good at ragtime. Very sweet. Not too noisy. But he was good.
When that band split up, who stayed with you? Which ones stayed with you and which ones went with Sillis?

Well, our band, we played at the Temple Roof Garden on a Wednesday night. Sillis Stain, the two Mareros and Paul Baum. They had a morning meeting. See? And the band, that's where they pulled out for me. Well, Lewis Madison, he was out among them and he heard of me. He called me up at 4 o'clock in the morning and he told me what they had done. But they had went out to Southern Yacht Club and told the secretary, Mr. Power and the president, Mr. Gossett, that I had quit playing music and turned everything over to them. That's what Celis Stain did. And so, next morning, I went down to the Southern Yacht headquarters. It was across from Beekman there. They had a...where they used to meet. And so, it was about 11 o'clock. And I got there. Well, Mr. Gossett said to me, well, originally, he said, what are you doing down here? I said, well, I just heard something blowing in the air, Mr. Gossett, and I come down to see about it. So, I heard that, they hired another band. He said, have you quit playing music? I said, no, sir. He said, you didn't quit playing music and turn everything...what did he say? Well, that Henry said Doug, the fella named, used to smoke those cigarettes and go out on the porch all the time. What is the name? Play cornet. I said, Celis Stain. He said, well, he was down there hitting the banjo player and they came down and told us that you had quit playing and turn everything over to them and we brought up a contract with them. Is that so? I told him, no, sir. He said, well, originally, how many of the band had you got? He said, is that girl playing with you? I said, yes, sir. He said, you got a drummer? I said, yes, sir. Well, I think I had a name fired. He said to the sonographer, he said, I want you to write that fellow Celis Stain a letter and tell him not to show up on the job Wednesday night. Because we have made that different arrangement with a different band. And then he wrote him that letter and he wrote me and he said, Ridley, say, you be out Wednesday night. Whoever you got, say, you bring them. So I went out and I had seven pieces and we went out and we did pretty good, but I know not that they had the band.
Do you use shots on trumpet? Shots.

Did shots. Yeah. And the shots I had been playing second with. He knows everything, you know. He could play a mirror and everything. He said, I'm going to play something. And so they came up and knocked off and said, people didn't know the difference. They said, some people thought of the same band. He said, we didn't tell them no better. He said, now you just come on out, sir, and practice up until you bring your band up again. They allowed me to build up another good band. And I got David Jones and another fellow. And we used to rummish listening out to the temple every time he come up there. He had a good band. We used to run him out every time he came down. My band, Richard Tuxedo Band, we used to play at the Pelican Grab and Rampo that time. They had a big dance hall and then they had the temple over there, roof garden. And we played against every band in the city of New Orleans up on that, up on the Pelican. We whipped every band up there. We whipped Jack Kerr at the National Park. We whipped Ory's band on a parade. We whipped them at the National Park at night. We whipped Rene, playing for a white dance. We had the privilege to whip every band that they had in the city. And people knew it. I don't care how good they was, whether people just liked us or the way we carried ourselves, that's one thing I did do. We carried a good band. Captain, kept them up on the spot all the time. They allowed me to drink. Not until after the dance. They didn't tell me to get us on the job. Nobody drank. We went down for lunch. We had something. That was all right. Nobody drank. Nobody smoked. Nobody get up on the seat until end of mission time. So that was what built us up. We had a very good band. I know something about us. It was as good as ours, but I think it's the way we carried ourselves, that people like this and that. We just got it over all of them. I was there with every corner player. Rene, Ory's corner player. What was playing with them? With them. With Rene, playing for white dance. I had my little thing. I knew somebody got it. I had a souvenir for each one of the dances I played. So I had the privilege to know that I did that.

Did they give cups sometimes? Like contests? A lot of people had one hander. Nice to see it. Anyway, you run those cups and all. We ripped them all. I was going to ask about the brass bands. If the tuxedo brass band marched on the street, the same fellows that played in the dance band, did you march on the street much?
Yes, I was one of the trombone players.
Were all the fellows in there? Were you manager of the brass band too?

No sir. I didn't have anything to do with the brass band. That was separate. That's Celestan. He took care of that and I took care of the orchestra. He didn't have anything to do with the orchestra, you see. So he done that to them there. Whatever was over, like a leader's shell like that, but we split on him and the job, you see, from him and I. But he didn't fool the orchestra at all, no longer when I was together. And I didn't bother with the brass band. They wanted to have to go see him.
Do you know when he organized that, was that as old as the dance orchestra or did it come up later?

The brass band? The brass band. Now, you mean the, it was along all the time we had that? Yes, is it way back? Oh yeah. It was way back then too. It was way back, the time when we organized the orchestra. Yeah, that could have been about a, a while after the auditions. It could have been around about 1970 or something like that. About that time. Yeah. Yeah, we had a good brass band and we used to put everybody on the street.
Who else played in the brass band? Did they have more than one trombone?
Yeah. You know him too, he got a leg cut up by the track. Oh, Sonny Henry.
Sonny Henry.

Him and I played together, we is. Very nice color. And, uh, it's the attitude trombone, him and I. Peter Biker, Peter Biker, one of the tronettes. Celestrian was one of the tronettes. When we first started playing, let me get that thing real. When we first started playing, we were with Henry Allen over the river, you see. We all used to play with him, you see. And then we'd pull up and, you know, and I, and we'd take, I met in the other fellas to take the tuxedo bands, you see. I met in the other band. So, he was a leader, he was a leader, Peter Biker. Peter Biker, Chuck played with us. I think we had three tronettes. Lorenzo Teo, clarinet player. Eddie Jackson, played tuba. Ernest Tafani, drum. And we used, you know, later when he died, then Happy came with us. Goldstein, his name is. He came with us. And, uh, Alto was Barbarang. Barbarang. Barbarang, old man. Barbarang. I don't know what he's playing at about. No, but he's still living. I guess he's as old as you, aren't you? Yeah, I think he's a little older than me. Him and Joe Piaier, I believe, was an old Alto player. He played wrestling many times.

We used Adolph Alexander on the Alto. Was that the young Adolph Alexander or his father? No, no. The young Alexander played with me once, you know, in my history. Yes. He played, coming playing saxophone, Tornet, and playing saxophone.

He played with me. He played with me. He played with me. I think he was a little older than me. I think he was a little older than me. Him and Joe Piaier, I believe, was an old Alto player. He played wrestling many times. We used Adolph Alexander on the Alto.
Is that the young Adolph Alexander or his father? No, no.

The young Alexander played with me once, you know, in my history. Yes. He played, coming playing saxophone, Tornet, and I was the one who got in to play saxophone. He started playing saxophone after he was with me. He didn't want to get on it. He didn't like it. The last step on behind him, he made good at it. He played saxophone. Arthur Durbany, he used to play with me.
The man in the band though, the Adolph Alexander, is that Tatt's father? That's right.
That's Tatt's father. He was a very good old timeist, isn't he? He was a kid.
I never knew him, I heard of him though.
He was good.
I was going to ask, did you ever play clarinet or started on clarinet when you were a boy?
I did have a clarinet, but I didn't, you know, didn't try to play it. I used to fit a round of wood, I didn't take no lesson.
Well you did have one when you were a boy. I had a clarinet. But you never did learn to play? No, I didn't. I didn't fool me that much.
See?
Did you have any other teachers besides Jim Humphrey when you were young? No.
Jim Humphrey was my starling. All the words that you could say was my everything, because he helped me a whole lot. I used to go around to his house and he was very good to me. He was a good teacher.
You were going to tell us about another older group that he taught too.

That was before my time, you see. I was around ten years old. I was just after my mother died. And I started waiting in that grocery place I was telling you about. And all of them used to gather there. The man we worked was a very good man. He always had a bunch of behind the very nice to cover people. And those boys got together and organized a band. And I think he paid for all the instruments, you know. That was twelve of them. I think he gave them all the instruments. They used to be at his place. But he used to keep it crowded all the time at the place, you see. And they used to rehearse a little there a couple of nights a week. And on Sunday, bless how we got to know Professor Jim Humphrey. See. And he used to come up there and teach George Brothers the same way. And I used to have to hold him when he was teaching them. A little old car that would come down and meet him. Take him back. See, and I still stayed there that band broke up. He was gone about six years before we started serving. And then I had to...
I hauled them the same way. I was joined then, I was in my 20s. I was over 20 when I started.
What kind of wagons did they have in those days when you'd bring them into town? Did they have surreys or carts?

No, they had a two-wheel spring cart, they called it. Two wheels? Two wheels, you know, with a spring on the spring. It wasn't what you call a dump cart, you know. No. The dump cart didn't have any spring, which was hard.
But this had springs on it.

But this had springs. We called it a spring cart, that's two wheels. And I used to haul them back and forth with that all the time. He helped me up and he talked to them on my way going back and forth. Even after I stopped getting listened for him, I used to meet him and he'd always have merit. A finer merit.
What kind of a trombone did you like when you played, what make did you use?

When they made up my mind to play trombone in the band, my people bought innocent model, I believe, the Vell, no, C.G. Kong. Kong. Vell, one Vell. I had a slide drum on me, they paid 85, I had to give it to me. So I had been with them.
Your first instrument was the slide then? No. Wait, I didn't get that straight.
My first instrument was the bass.
It was the bass, I mean your first trombone then. My first trombone was slide.
The slide.
But it had a trill valve.
Yes. See? I think they called it the end of the trill valve on a Kong trombone, C.G. Kong trombone. It had one vowel.
One vowel.
It was a trill valve. One vowel, yeah. Oh, it went out of the start, I don't think it made so much of a hit.
True valve, did you say something? The one vowel. Just the one for trill.
The slide. For the trill, I see. Yeah, it should.
Oh, yeah, I see.
That's a nice idea. Yeah, I never saw one of those.
I don't think the last one, no. I don't think that was a good make. Did you... I didn't see any others but that one.
Did you have more than one trombone or I mean that was just...
In life, I bought here, I had three trombones. Oh, yeah.
What make did you get next after? Always...

No. The last one was Holt. Holton? A brass. A brass. A brass, yeah. A brass. And then I didn't have that long before I quit. And had a fellow playing the... Used to go through every yard on a circus like that. He was one of those circus trombone players. And I was getting ready to start playing trombone. And on his way through on the circus, I asked him about playing. And he said he had to go to Tulsa Oklahoma to put his shoe up. And when he get there he was riding it. So he did. And I brought him on to New Orleans, you see. And he played trombone while I was trying to play a drum. Yes. And I sold it to him for $25. He paid me $5. But the reason I gave it to him, because when he got there, I didn't have the weight that I thought I would have had, you know, to give him. And he didn't have a good horn. So I didn't give him a horn show and let him go over somebody else. He did that.
I was going to ask some more about the Silverleaf Band. What kind of music they played? Did they play ragtime or was it more blues? Did they use sheet music all the time?

They used sheet music. Yeah, well I'll tell you. See, Albert Baptiste, he led the Silverleaf Band when I first started for a while. And then he was a coffee potter. He worked for O'Keeffe on Magazine Street. That case. Yeah. And it kind of helped with his job. So then he turned over to Oscar Randall. I guess you remember him.
Oscar?

Randall. He was a pretty good violin player. And so he took up several of his bands and Albert's players for a while because the band began to draw a little bit and waking up, he couldn't get out to sheet. And so he had to let somebody else play. So Oscar Randall, he took it then. And we played sheet music. Wasn't much on the ragtime. Did you ever play anything by ear at all?
Did you ever play anything by ear at all? Without reading from the music? Did you ever play anything by ear at all? Without reading from the music?

Plenty of time. You did plenty of time. You did plenty of time. You know we used to make those wagging at the time and give them things like that. That's why we couldn't use no music at that time. No. You know we'd buck. You know we'd come on to some time, bands would buck for about a half an hour you know. And like that but you couldn't use no music there. You had the gut bucket. Because most of it was anything you could do, anything you could move.
What pieces did you play then?

Well most of those they've come to places like there was something. They played plenty of blues you know like St. Louis Blues. Nella was one of our main hosts. The other bands couldn't play it. They didn't know how we got it you see. Of course that was the number we fixed. The piece of music was Nella, that was the name of it. Well we cut the name off you see. And Tom Burton, we used to play a reggae and one night we were always playing, had a good crowd of people playing color dance. They had a couple of drinks in them. And we used to make a break in that hooey and Nella you know. We made the... We stopped there. And so he started to have drunk one night. And so when we made that break he said... We said oooey. And we kept that up.
And we made it. And made it.
And made it.
And made it.

And made it. And he got laughed over and sat so many times. Yeah. She made it. And he said oooey. And the people who didn't know. We just had to play. And nobody know where it comes from. What else was going to do. They never did know how to play. And we kept like that's the last job. And that's the moment we kept in the job all the time. And we used to play that. And that was a scream. And none of them couldn't play. And then the...
That was the Silver Leaf that did that.
Oh. That was the original Tuxedo band.
Oh that was the original Tuxedo.
Oh we'd go in big dance. Silver Leaf.
Well I was wondering the difference. Did the Silver Leaf sound much different than the... Original Tuxedo? Original Tuxedo? Oh.
Oh much different. Nice different.
What was the difference? Did they play different kind of music?
But the men could just... But we all had to improve. Even myself.
Yeah sure you'd improve. I wondered though.

And then we had different ideas you know. Better ideas. You know how to make different own arrangements like that and practicing. And we used to get to... Oh Graff one I believe we called it you know. And something come out like that where the other bands would be playing. But we would just have a practice like that. We called it special practice when we had one fella playing a clarinet named Ezebri Zanaris. Lana Rees. And he could catch those records. He played C clarinet. And he could catch those records. Those records you could see. And we'd always come over and some morning before they get in there. Tell them all right I'd do the same thing. But they never get away. And who would not. We used to practice things on them. And they'd always come over and some morning before they get in there. And tell them all right I'd do the same thing. And they'd never get away. And who would not. We used to practice things on them. Plenty of nights. Good places just to come out and meet the other bands like that. And put it down if they didn't do it. But we always did have something new. Trying to satisfy the people. I was still I don't like to worry about that. No I'm not worried. That the. Mojaspin Mojaspin Mojaspin. But I wonder what kind of pieces did they play. Well they seemed music. They was pretty good but most straight you know. Were they waltzes? Marks. Marks. Marks.
Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks.
Marks. Marks. Marks. Marks.
Were they waltzes? Marches there?
Were there waltzes?
Were there waltzes?

Were there waltzes? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there?
Were there qual된 stuff there?
Were there qual된 stuff there? Were there qual된 stuff there?
Were there qual된 stuff there?

No, not that time it was gone. We didn't play. It's gone already. Yeah, now if we, we have played quadrilles for different dancers like that, special dancers, but the people would ask for them and we just get some boots and practice them up, you know. But that wouldn't, we didn't use that in no way as else. But that was always gone. But when we come along during the Charleston time, we could play that. We could play the Charleston days.
Did the Silver Leaf ever play blues much? Yeah. They played blues too. They played blues.
Or they had to do it. Yes. See, they had to play some kind of blues.

I was going to ask about the very first bands you remember playing, hearing, before you took up music. Did that, up in the country, were any of the New Orleans bands up there? John Robichaux. John Robichaux.

See, John Robichaux. And I heard them all because, you see, I worked at that grocery, and whenever they give dancers, every band had to pass that store to get where they was going to play in, in the little place back there most of them. And they all used to stop there and play at the stores, advertising there, you know. Yes. They'd stop there and play a couple of tunes, and we'd give them a couple of drinks, you see. And then they'd leave and they'd go. That's where they had to go. But the Robichaux band played well in a different place from there, you see. I used to go over there. Back to the Lille, the first slum drum, slide trumpet player. No, no. Tucker. A fellow by the name of Tucker. What do you know? Tucker. Tucker.
Tucker. Tucker. It was the first slide. Slide trumpet player I had to sing.

But that wasn't long. I was a boy. I was around about 18. And I used to go up to the guy and play. He was with John Robichaux band then. That's the time they had old Brad Frank playing a piccolo. He was a wonderful piccolo from memory. He didn't play anything. He was good. And then that's Robichaux band. You see. John Robichaux. I believe Andrew Kimball. I think Bud Scott was playing banjo from there. What's up with him? I don't know. They didn't have any drums at that time. Didn't have the drums. No. You know the trap drums. They didn't have them. They didn't have the trap drums coming out of Lincoln Park. We had got trouble with the question. I started with that. Didn't have any drums. But it was good. That's the first band. I'm quiet out there. But all the rest of the band played and stopped at that store. I know the mighty old musicians in New Orleans just stopped at that store.
Did you play with Louie Cottrell in your band ever?

Yeah. He played a while with us. I tell him and Pierron went to Chicago for a while. Louie, I think Teo, Grantio, Pierron, I think Joyce, no not Teo didn't go, but Joyce Backhead. Joyce Backhead. Yes. Joyce Backhead. There was four or five of them left here. But they didn't stay very long up there. But that's when Louie Cottrell had them playing with us. That's why he got away from Muslin, you see. I remember the Chicago.
Did you ever hear Buddy Bolden's band? Do you remember?
Yes sir. I remember Buddy Bolden being good. Him and John Robeshow, at that time it was just them two bands, I believe, bucking at each other. Most of it I knew of. He worked very good.
Where did you hear Bolden? Was he up in Jefferson or down here?

Heard him in Jefferson, heard him down here. See? Heard him down there. Heard him down there. Heard him down there. Heard him down there. Heard him down there. Heard him down there. Yeah Lincoln Park. Heard him down there. Yeah Lincoln Park. Robeshow played. And there were many places where they both played.
Who was his trombone player in Bolden, do you know? When you heard them?
Let me see. I believe he had a vowel trombone player by the name of Ed Jones.
Ed Jones played vowel trombone.
Yeah he was good. Good vowel trombone player. You know he played. Plenty Headway and Boyle at Plenty Headway.
I don't know him. Somebody told me once that Carnish had played with him. Do you remember Carnish? Carnish, yeah I know him good.

You knew him? He played with Boyle too. I think Ed Jones was the first. Well between him and Carnish, I know where Carnish played with him. And I know Ed Jones played with him. And the both was good. Yeah, Carnish played with him.
Did Frankie Doosen ever play with Bolden? Do you remember?

Not as I know of. No, I don't know. I don't think Frankie Doosen would play with Bolden. Maybe he was. He could have played with him, but I don't remember him. But he was a good old trombone player too. He had plenty headway with him. Not much of a year. Plenty headway.
Can you tell me about, some more about Baptiste de Lille? I never got to know him. He died long before my time. I wonder. No, I don't think so.
He uh...
I didn't live here you see until a few years ago, so I never knew him.
But this is what happened to him. He uh, went out of the audible mile. Oh I believe I heard that. And he stayed in Jacksonville about 14 or 15 years.
Really?
That ball? I didn't know. And then when he came back, you know he pinned up on the trombone. Just like that. And played again?
Yeah. Was he really very good? Good.
Was he good? He was a good trombone player. Very good musician. Fine man, band man.
Do you know about when he died? How long he's been gone?
No, not too long, but less than 10 years about that.
That's about all.

I didn't know. I didn't know. Very good. Now, he stayed in Jackson 14 years, but his wife wouldn't send him to get him. And I don't know how he got here, but when he got here, he wasn't alone, she died. Well I know two men that happened there.
Yeah, strange.

I know another oldwood parish like that. A man's wife was in Jackson and she was writing the little son to get him. And the church sent him and got him. And when she come home, he's gone about 15, 16 years. And when she come, he died about a year. So after that. That's great. He wouldn't send him to get her.
Did Leo play slide all the time or at one time? Very good.
I didn't know him when he played the guy, but I think he did. You only heard him on the slide then? Yeah, that was at Lincoln Park then. Yeah, that was at Lincoln Park then.
Tip

That's when we used to have Buddy Bowling playing what's called Johnson Park and Robichaud playing and Lincoln Park. There was about four blocks separating each other, you see. So that's where I know both of those from. I used to visit those places, but I would live in Indiana. I was a boy.
Can you remember any other members of that Bowling band at that time?

Remember any clarinet? Let me see, I know they had the guitar player. We called him Brock, I believe his name was Brock Umford. But that was the only man I can remember in Bowling band. I'm sure I knew more of them, but they've gone from my name now.
Can you remember about what instruments he used?
How many were in the band did he use?

At that time, the most he used was, he didn't have no drums, played back there, you know. But after when Bowling came up, I did the head drum. He used to have plenty of playing with only five pieces, sometimes four.
Four or five, something. Yeah, four or five. Did he use a string bass? Yeah, always used string bass.

Always used the bass. Bass. Plenty of time he only had bass, banjo, tronet, maybe clarinet. I think. Plenty of time he played four pieces. Plenty of time he played five, six like that. The most of it was six pieces back in the old days, you see. And then I think the first seven piece band I saw was when John Wilkinshire went out to the Lincoln Park. And Louis Kattrall got to play in the trap drum. I think that's what the first seven piece band I saw.
Do you remember what kind of a trumpet player Bowling was, kind of a quartet or anything he was?
Good.
He was a good player.

Good. Very loud and strong, you know, and could just play a long time, you know. But he was good. Nothing, always a king Bowling. That's what he could get, but he was very good. Always had a crowd that he played, you know.
You know, what kind of music he played, was it more ragtime than they have today or what?
No, than a rag. But on the same water almost, you know.
Would it sound modern today, about like the jazz bands or Dixieland bands play today? No, but no.
The stars did be a little bit different, you know, with that double beat and so on like that. So we didn't have the effect like the band got now, but it was good, you know, at that time.
What do you mean by the double beat? Was that a slower beat or faster beat? Faster, you know, faster. Faster, faster.
That's the stars. See, we hit the beat most of the time, you know. Time like that, 2-4, you do one, two and so on that.
Like in 2-4, that's the way the Tuxedo band played. No, no, not, no.
I'm talking about way back on it.
Oh, the bold, the bold band played slower, the two beats.
Right, and when I first started learning, and there was teaching us, you see. Yeah. But after that, they usually turn and do that.
Then they begin to use the double, double time. Yeah, double time.
I have to gain that double time. So we was doing that too, before I started. But David Jones, you see, when he come playing saxophone with me, he had been, we were on the boat together, see.
Yes.

And when I came back to Noir on the boat, I went to see him close, David went to New York. And when he learned that stuff in New York, so when he come here with our band, he know the whole lot of stuff that the college didn't know. So he learned that double beatin' that fast time and all like that and the people liked it, you see.
Yes, I see.
Yes, it sounds dope. David, he was very good at that. I think he's teaching in California now. I don't think he's playing in the band. He's out somewhere around where Johnny Sinceri is.
Yes, that's what I hear. He's out in California now.

And they say he's a little gray head man now. Well, he was getting the gray head at that time, but anyway you touched him was music. Anyways, he just had it. He was a fine fellow. All those old times, things like that. Now Jim Humphrey, how you can remember, I liked it a long, long time. The old brass band, when you taught that old brass band, he used to write, you see. He used to write it for him at that time. And it was easier for him to get an intern, you see. I did write. I knew he was a good old corner player, and he had a very good, the boy had a couple good corners to catch quick. And whatever he'd bring, they'd catch it, you see. And then he'd go right off with.
But Jim Humphrey would bring a new piece each week then, written out.
No, he'd written it out, yeah. That is, quick he could teach a band, fast, you see.
Were those all marches, or were some of the sort of jazz numbers too?

Marches, marches. That brass band at that time, they hadn't got to play no dance music. That's all they wanted to play a march. But he hadn't done pretty good. But I think they lost a good corner player that wouldn't go to the advantage when he died. They were doing fine. Well, they were the same way people that helped me, helped them. You see, I worked on a job, started when I was about 12 years old, and I worked there until I was around, I was about 18 years. And I did everything. I worked in the grocery, I was a porter, I was a yard boy, you know, I was a nut cow. I used to sell in the grocery bar. I used to help, oh, I grew up doing that kind of work. That's why when I'd take me over being the manager of the tuxedo band, wasn't no strange BBC, because I'd been the white people all my life. I was just trying, I was just hard to go, and I was well trained. I had that good old Dixie train, and you see, I know it's not fair. I just went along, I tried to be a nice, colorful, and that helped me a whole lot. I could talk pretty good, you know, tried to be as nice as I could, and I think it helped me a whole lot. So I was well trained, I was still with Jeremy's family, I nursed the children, I did everything.

I was going to ask a little bit more about your family. If any other members of the family, any uncles or anyone played music? You say your father didn't play, didn't you? No. I had two brothers played.
Were they older? Older than me, older. And they went to the American-Spanish War. They played in the U.S. Band.
So they didn't use the music in his band. Did they play any dance music ever? I don't think.
Which instruments did they play? One played baritone, one played alto.
Do you remember, can you, actually, you know their name, what were their names?

One, Manier Richley, that's my brother, and my other was U-S-A-M, U-S-A-M. I like my daddy. See? He played baritone. He was pretty good baritone. But there wasn't nothing in it much for dancing. They didn't make that. So they didn't.
Who would you see? They wanted to work. I was going to ask, is that how you got your sort of nickname, your little name?

Big Baby? Big Baby. That's, and I'm telling you brothers, they're famous too. That's what, no hollerin' about, no my name was William. They'd be a rich little. That's all they called them. Everybody, even their white people, you see, go. They got their called in there. Now when I started, around up where I live, like up here, and called them, well I used to play all the little white parties and everything. And they all know they know they're probably good because they didn't even before I ever come to New Orleans and wait for the other white people, you see. So I never went to play any white people over here before I came to New Orleans, you see. I've been with them a long time. So all they know was Bebe, Bebe. They went to New Orleans, Bebe, Bebe. Got some of them coming in to Bebe and got some little children out there. I don't know what they call Mr. Bebe. I get kicked.
Is that from the French, the French name, the way they pronounce it Bebe? No, no. It's from my sister. She used to call me Habele.
Oh yeah. And from that, she started to call me Bebe, one of my sisters. I don't even know what she called. That's what Bebe means. Bebe.
Yes, I see. That's what she got there.
How do they spell that when you're writing? Bebe. Bebe. Bebe. Bebe. Bebe. Bebe. Bebe. Bebe. Bebe.

That's Bebe Ridgely. Bebe Ridgely. That's all. And I know I think I'm exaggerating. I didn't tell wherever they played. They said Bebe Ridgely, Texas Band of New Year, there's a drum. I drew a crowd. I just don't know. I don't know, just a blessing from God, but I always drew and got along good with the people. Oh yeah.
I was going to say, how many were there in your family? How many brothers and sisters did you have?

Thirteen of us. Thirteen. Thirteen. I don't know. But I knew the last two. See, my mother died, well I was the largest one at home. The others died before my time, I didn't know them. See, I didn't know none of them. I only know six of us. Yeah. See, six years. But when my mother died, I was the largest one at home. All my two brothers had us gone. Then I had two sisters and a brother, younger than me. And my mother had twins after that, and they died babies, you see. My mother died in childbirth, she had a dropship. And she died for most two kids. So that was before that I didn't know nothing about it. But they were special. I played for each other.
Yeah.

I wanted to ask some more about the records you made, those first records you told about, when Manuel Moneta played piano, and the shots on that date too. Two coronet, shots on the cellar stage. Used two coronets.
Shots led, what's he call the name there, well. It was Careless Love.
Careless Love. Oh, shots. Shots.

Plays the lead in Careless Love. See, he was fairly good and smooth. And ragtime, he had a touch, you know, he had a real good touch on the corner. He was one of them, Tim used to like to play him, he used to always ask him to play the blues, play Kellers Love and all that. Whoever went like that, there was always somebody asking shots to play something, you see. And he played Kellers Love. And he was very good.
And I wonder, did you make more records after that? No.

Well, we didn't even, in fact, we didn't follow them. But I don't know who got the money on them, the secrets or something. I had to be separated. I don't know. I think John Morello, he tried to get the money. I don't know what they got. We didn't know nothing but, didn't know how to go about nothing like that. Yeah, I see. And so we just got beat out of that.

But are those the only records that you made then? Yeah, on them. Those are the only records? Yeah, I think. Because I think Celestan went ahead and they made some more for Columbia later, but you weren't on any of those Columbia. No, I wasn't even with them.
He got a, must have a four or five of them, I guess.
Yeah, I think there were several.

Yeah, he did well. Oh, he made money. He made dollars while I made pennies. He got no money when he was playing like when he was playing. He was a fine fellow. Good cornet player. Nice man. Good fellow. I tried to get him to quit playing. He wouldn't quit a little like this so much. I tell him, I said, son, you're getting so old. I said, you made a reputation out there, ain't I? I said, now you got a little bit of money. I said, I didn't have anything when I quit. I said, even my home was, the morris. I said, I didn't have anything. I didn't know what I was going to do. I didn't quit all the night. I said, I made it. I said, you can make it. I didn't do it. But I know he didn't like this so much. But the last words he said to me, I used to go down to the house on Grand Street. Go down there and I'd sing and I'd pray for him. He said, Ridley, if I ever get over there, I'll never pick up that horn again. I didn't say nothing in, but I thought. But he did that anyway. I said, I thought to myself too, but I used to tell him, I said, you old man? I said, you got a few dollars in my city. Got a little income? And I said, you can't keep on playing. And that dancing, going on like he was an old man and got seven years old and working hard all his life and all that. He didn't use, he said that people like it. I said, all right. So when they had him over here in the hospital, all the two damn mountain, he'd find out. And he sent for me, told the lady to come over there and pray for him. She told me, but this time of evening, I guess. I said, well, it's too late now. I was there first thing next morning. And he was there to see me and the doctor was so nice to him. I went in and I slept in a long while, I called him, and sang, prayed, and everything. And then when he went back down to his house, I did the bus and I used to get around there. And I would pray with him and do everything. But the last word he said, I heard him speak, he said, if I get over this, I'll never pick up that horn again. I thought too late because I knew that they had an outbreak on him, what's called a cancer. You see, because my wife.
I never knew what he died from. He said it, cancer. I didn't know.

My wife died. He canceled the blood. And I knew from the way that she said there was, you know, sakesing for her. And he told me, and they were doing the same thing with him, you see. And I said, they're looking for cancer. So I was in there and the doctor came in and said, they said, well, Selv, can I have you, old boy? And I said, he says, everything's all right, doctor? And the doctor said, yes. He said, we found out. He said, we found out.

That's what we want to find out about it." I said, yeah. He said, we're thinking we can do something right. The doctor said, only one little thing, Rick. He said, we got a little small operation. He said, it ain't much. He said, just a little operation when we get that. And I thought they had cancer. I said, I was sitting there. I said, cancer. Sighting for cancer. And sure enough, they operate on them next week. And after they operate on them, they send them home. And he told me when they were sending them home, they said, the doctor, when must I come back? So the doctor said, we'll send them for you. It was time. I thought again. Oh, he was suffering. He was suffering. He said he was sorry. He let them operate on them. And how did he get over it? Another couple days after he died.

Well, I don't want to bother you much longer. I guess you're getting tired. No, you're bothering me. I'm going to ask, if you have a few minutes, to tell us about some of the other trombone players. Because a lot of those old timers I wouldn't know about. Well, if you could tell us some more about Carnish.
Carnish was a good reading trombone player.
He wasn't a good reader.

No. But he had a good ear. See? He played mostly by the... Frankie Duesen wasn't a good reader. But he had a good ear. See? Poor ear. At the time he was... He wasn't a good reader. But I believe he picked up there. I think he reads pretty well now, they say. I believe.
No, no.

He wasn't a good reader. Still playing, you know? Yeah. He was doing good and making money. He wasn't reading trombone player. But he was good. See? He could catch a thing and play a good one on it already. You don't worry about that. Either one of them. Yes. He was good. And Vic Gastra, fine trombone player. Buddy Johnson, fine. And Buddy Johnson's brother, Yank, he called him. He was a good trombone player. Then the fellas came up back to give my time. I'm trying to tell you about it, but I don't know what it was late ones. Henry Charles, Sonny Henry. He was good. Then we had an old, old trombone player way back there on the Joe Pitti, old trombone player. He was good. What was his name again?
Joe Pitti.
Joe Pitti, sure. He used to be with the... I knew him.
That's right.

I knew him. He was with the... The clarinet player downtown. What's his name? Old, old, old man. Piku? Piku. Them was brothers, you see. Them was two fellas. And you hired them to play and somebody would say, well, we're going to have a third of supper at Kawano over there. And they said to somebody. Piku, you blow up anybody's job to go drink wine. He's a fine fella. I like Piku, yeah. He's good. Nice fella. Funny. Comical. Could not tremble on for his... I don't see...
How was Beth DeLeo? Was he a good reader? Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.

He was a master, dear, above us all. He was a master, huh? Yeah, I'm a master. Yeah, but the fella Tucker, when I tell him about it, I live way back in the... No, you don't know him. I just know him by name, see him play, and I didn't know him. But he was a good, too.
Did you know Zoo Robertson?
Fine trombone player. Fine, but I forgot about him. Fine, fine player.
I knew him in California before he died. He's dead now. He's dead now. He died 15 years ago.
Yeah.

I don't know. He wasn't a good mixer somehow or another, you know. He was very good musician, everything like that. He never had much to say, you know. They'd go and play the music playing for you from the front of him. Mm-hmm. See?
Another trombone player from New Orleans I knew in Chicago, Roy Palmer. Did you know Roy? Played him and I played together. Oh, you did?
We were playing together when he lived in Chicago. That's when Sonny Henry came in. He was good. Is he living?
Yes, he's living. He still works in the steel miller. He looks strong. I saw him about three years ago.
He always was strong. He was good and strong. And there was good trombone player, too.
I never got to hear except his records. He had a good head, huh? He was good.
He was good. He was good.
Oh, George Field. I never got to meet him. I think he got on police force. He got to be a detective. Who was your favorite of all the trombone players? He died in Chicago.
He died in Chicago. George Field.
Did you know him? I was a trombone player, too, wasn't he? Yes, from downtown.
He played with Manuel Perez a lot.
Yeah, yeah. That's right. George Field. He was good.

Real good. I never got to know him. I never heard him. I think when he left, I think he got on police force in Chicago. I think he got to be a detective. Him, a Tucker, he was one of us. I think George Field. I was a Tucker. I think I got on police force. He got to be a detective.
Who was your favorite of all the tromboners when you were young that you liked to listen to?

Well, I'll tell you, I used to love the old man Big Jasper. He was nice on trombone. Smooth, I played. But there was a further noise there. It was all the light, you see. So you'd get a kink out of them and see they could raise so much playing on that trombone. They'd give you a good time. You were a reading fellow, a good time. Yeah. Especially out in the street and everything I think I thought, but they had no stuff like you. I used to love the old man Jack Carey. He didn't know. Watch, I forgot.
I was going to ask about Jack Carey. How was he? He was a real good, uh-oh.
He wasn't a good reader. He was a spart. Not a good reader, no? Oh, but a kiss.
See, them kind of guys that went on his way out.

Catch it that quick, huh? Anything. And then he got asked, you know, he got to go. He got to go. He got to go. Anything. And then he got to add to it, you know. Yeah. Add and take away from it. Ordered it like that. Prydips like that. Fully-carnished it like that. Some kind of guy.
You said a little earlier that you used to play Tiger Rag. Was that Jack Carey's speciality or something like that?
In the beginning.
Yeah, it's almost saying.
In the beginning, you see. He got it from a record, you know. Yeah. He was the first one that started playing it from the record. Yeah. And he used to wash off of that too.
Did Jack Carey play it before the original Dixieland, do you think, or after their record? Yeah. Before. Before the? Yeah. But you think he heard it on a record too, or what?
Well, he had to sure heard it on the record. We didn't get no other way, but he got it on the record. Somebody asked to hear it, I don't know if he played it.
How far back, when did you first hear it that you can remember? Was it before the war or during the war, after the First World War? I think after the First World War.
After the First World War. I think so, yeah. They came back. Tiger Rag.

I didn't know when it came out, if they played it down here years before the war or not. Some people told me they played it a long time before. I never knew though, I thought you would know, because you were here and playing music. I don't know if you were here, the First World War has been about how long? About 1914 when they started the war, and it was over in 1918.
I'll give you about what, about how many years?
About four years during that First War lasted. Well, no. That was 50 years ago.
No, we weren't playing Tiger Rag at that time. Weren't playing it?
No.

What was that show? Mm-hmm. That came out after. Mm-hmm. And Jack caught up from a, buying a record, you know, he caught up in there. And he used to play, when he first come out, wouldn't want nobody to play with him. And he'd get us out on the street playing an appetite and get us on the corner. He'd play nothing to Tiger Rag.
He'd do that sort of Tiger Rag, or they...

And then, the Tiger Rag is good until the day, and we all had to play it a whole lot of time. But I don't know, we had something about us. People used to like our style of playing, buddy. You know, they had the big white parties and all that kind of stuff. They didn't have them bands. None of them. And I had the afternoon. I used to play a tuxedo band. I used to play all of the carnival bars. I played most of all of the carnival bars. I started in World War I, playing for Dr. O' Kelly, playing for the 12-night revels. Every carnival day, at the 7th of January, I just had to have a brother in at the Boston Club, you see. Let him know that I remember that day. He never said no better than let me, you see. Just to know the choir. I played for the Boston Club. I started on Thursday night. I played Monday night, Tuesday all day, Monday, Monday night, Tuesday all day, and Tuesday night. We played that where the king used to come in, you see, and have a little sip. Oh yeah. We played that band there every year. See, nobody got it but us. See, I know that was my job. And then the 6th night reveling, oh, that, Captain Cook was ahead of that. He was dead, an old man. All I had to do was to write him a letter. I knew that it was going to be the 6th of January. But during the war, when things was dull and people was crying like that, they had two dancers a year. Six and eight, twelve and eight, that way. We used to play that at the carnival, at the men. Yes.
Did you play any of the parades during carnival too? Yes sir.

Yes sir. All we were at on the parade. Outside, the carnival day after we got to play in Boston Club, we couldn't play that no more, you see. So we used to play in the club. So we used to go and make that the parade then. I played it and I knew the tabloids, I knew how to connect the tabloids, that's a big ball at the afternoon. Is that the French Opera?
Did you ever play at the French Opera House, those balls? Yes. Never played those. No.
No. That's before my time I think. But I, you see that's when they come to the acronym, I think the French Opera was playing.
Yes, after that burned down.

Well I used to play all the ball and I knew all the tabloids, tabloids. See, after some stand you knew it, you see. You didn't know how to conduct the tabloids. See they used to practice me, you see. I would go down, like I was going to play a dance next week, I had to go down, especially to a meeting and look at them, see. Then I'd have to take the band. Yeah. So I had to come back and play the band. Then I'd take them down. I knew I'd connect all the tabloids, the Camelot Jenkins. I played one of the largest dancers, Oriental dance, the Camelot Jenkins. I'd say, oh, after me. You remember y'all never played there? Yes. I used to know nobody played there but me. My band did everything. Oh, I had a wonderful name. Well I'll tell you gentlemen, I had a grandmother died in 103 and she used to pray for me. I was going to never have bad luck on the dying day. She said, yeah, I'll never have bad luck. And I made a nice living. I've never been convicted of anything. I've never been in jail. I've never been in no kind of trouble. Nothing like that. And I've always made a living among the best people, colored and white. I always had one of the names among the white people. That's right.
People tell me that too. It was a popular band, that tuxedo. Popular. I just kept on straight.

They didn't really like it. Some of them used to fuss with me. Some night when they get up, that guy said, you have to get to play and say, I'm hungry. I said, you're hungry? I said, didn't you know you were just coming with the white? And then he didn't know. I said, you need to tell me you can't go about two hours and a half before you're in the mission or three hours or something. He said, no, get out. He said, once more, no slas. He said, no slas. He said, you're in the mission. They get hot with me. But I'm telling you, I made more money from him. I made more money from him. But that's the best time. So everyone knew they weren't going to leave. But you just had to be like that. I didn't mean that. But you got to bluff a little bit sometimes. Sometimes. If you don't care if they could reach you, they'll do you. Yes. I didn't let them go. They felt like smoking it going down straight. I said, what are you doing? No, no. And now, the guy smoked a bed. I said, who are you? Smoking one this thing? I said, where did you get that head? I said, well, they smoked one this thing. I said, you want a sign. You got to be glad you done with these kind of people. I said, you ain't going to smoke one this thing. I said, you ain't going to smoke one. I had a brother, John. He was a good drummer. And he used to get a little lordy sometimes. When he didn't show up, I'd leave for him to get. I'd sing him back a couple of times. He'd been drumming and gone back home. Never come home. He'd never do nothing to show me up. The people would come out there and tell him any kind of stuff. I said, well, I said, he's got a big deal. He's got a big deal. He's got a big deal. He's got a big deal. I was wondering, when you first started out, how much money the musicians made?
What did they pay for dances?
Silver leaf, for instance, way back those days.
Good question.

When we first started playing, we used to play all around, all the little white dance and everything like that, ten dollars and a half. Three hours. A dollar and a half for men and two hours for the leader. And we played a many again. Ten and a half for the whole band. The whole band. And when we played in the district, we'd be getting down a half a night, but we made two. And I went out on the job, went outside like that. The color dancers used to run from eight to count to the four in the morning. Two and a half a man, three dollars for the manager. And then when we got on up to playing the white school dance and things like that, we used to get five dollars a man. We used to get thirty-six dollars for our band. One dollar over.
That was a tuxedo.

That was a tuxedo band. But we was coming up all the time. Yes. You see. So when we stopped playing, we'd get seven, eight dollars on the job paid through. We used to play a key at three and get to the next key for five thirty and get to the next job for now. See, my brothers, way back then they used to be able to make, see when they leave home they'd come back at about eighteen dollars. You see, but none of that other band couldn't do that. They were big at that time, you see. And we'd play at the carnival ball, the big Boston club. We'd get fifteen dollars a man a day to leave in. So then I got twenty-five, down a day. See, I got fifteen. That was well understood. So I said, I carried everything and I used to manage it and keep in mind.

We were in good shape. Never was laid on her job. Never had no trouble. Went all through the state of Louisiana. All hours of night, anywhere. Plenty of time we had to sleep in the railroad station. Nobody would go and get a room. Miscuitis used to eat us up. But we never had no trouble. Nobody would ever bother. We went all over the car, the crack of town and everything else. Then we never did bother. We had a job in Central Hotel one night. There wasn't iron colored bands in there. We got in and the people wouldn't let them put us out. That's it. They put these bands out there. After that they sent high.
That's good. I wonder, did you save any of your old music? Your old orchestrations that you used with the tuxedo band?

When did you know? That's right. When I quit and joined church, I didn't want anything to do with gasoline and water. They didn't have mix. So I said, if I was going to try and save God. That's right. He said, you either farm or you're against him. Whether you're with him or against him. See? So I had a hard plane, a tractor farm for me. He came up with an automobile and I loaded him up.
Well, I loaded it up.

I wouldn't even want him to teach a boy drummer. I even wouldn't do that. I didn't want nothing to do with it. So I never did try to fool with it. I never did try to play. I took one job after I quit and joined church. I used to play there in Baton Rouge, you know, LSU's place. Oh yeah. All the way to play at regular. So the man was so nice to us. And I had my truck. I used to make 25 dollars to haul the band, you see. But I won that 25 dollar. So I took one job and went up there and played it. And I had to sit right there with the band. So I just got up there and I didn't like it.

I wondered if you saved any of the old pictures. Do you have that one picture there with Clarence Williams and all. I have a copy of that I got from Johnny St. Cyr. Do you have any other old pictures that you saved from the bands?
Well, I had one I'd give it to my cousin. I had a good picture. Most I got now I did my own pictures. So I got some of them if you want to look at that. Yeah, didn't I?

There was one picture I saw once with your tuxedo band with the... in a book that was published one time. I didn't know if you still had that one or not. Oh, I was going to ask you, did you ever play in that big, during the Depression, that big WPA band, you know, they had. Did you ever play in that?
I was out then. I quit. You'd quit by that time already? I quit. I didn't switch.

About what year was that you quit? 1931 or when was it? About 31. About 31 then. Yes. Yes, that was then before the WPA band. Who did you say you loaded his car with, the saxophone player you said? With all the sheet music and that?

Yeah, I did medicine. Who was that? I don't know. He didn't know the boy. No? I didn't. I just forgot it. And he asked me if I had that, I gave him something up on the music yet, man. And I said, come up there, we got out of my beer. And I gave him everything. I didn't want nothing to do with it.
So, we're trying to...
I made a pretty good... I got along pretty good by being in the saxophone. I think I made the best move. You see? I've made all those old fellas who are gone.
Fred, you're one of the few that's left of your age. The only one trouble I'm blessed was my time ago. And all of them. All of them were gone. I think I'm an only one there.
Henry, Sonny Henry. Yeah, he was a bad move. But he was always pretty strong. And I think sometime, I say, well, maybe add a little something to my life.
Right. Anyway, if you're happy, that's the way to be. Happy. Very happy. You look happy.

That's it. Happy. I got along, I got plenty of friends on both sides. I'm sorry that I... I don't know why I did it. I wanted to show you... I got some rep-ins. You see? I wanted to show you all. I wanted to show you a record that where I worked when I was a boy. See? And it says... like this. It says... I left one on my own account. Well, that many people was... the one that helped me. I had nobody. I had no mother, no father. Nobody that helped me. Those white people, they helped me. And I got a record from them. And he was very good.
Your father died when you were young, too.

Yeah, when I was young. He wasn't a good father, though. And my mother was good. And I wanted to show you all, though. I got a record from New Orleans Country Club. I played all of that stuff. I got Southern Yacht. Wonderful records. I got records from Wurline. I got Wurline from Dave or what you call him at the... Frank. Frank. Nice letter. Now, he was the man who used to write around the time when I wanted to call it, like David and Sears would open. I'd have nice cards printed, you see. Well, he used to fix me the cards from me. I got a nice letter card from him. Nice envelope. And I'd look in the telephone book. I'd look in the paper. And I'd get the people that's gonna have the... Debutary and daughter, go in and make something like that. Well, I'd send them a card. I'd send cards all over the city. I'd get about 500 of them or more, you know.
Did that have your picture on the band, that card or anything?
No, we didn't have that anymore. Just a... Just a nice card. Yes. And he used to fix them for me all the time. He was very good to me, too.

Well, we're just about out of tape here. And that's some other question that... Do you have anything, Ralph, that you could... Want to ask about? No, I don't think so. Is there anything else that you wanted to tell us? I think you've told us your whole life now pretty well, as originally. Can you tell me something I put it in? Yes, it's very fine. I'm just sorry I didn't have those letters for sure going on.
Well, that's alright. I understand what those letters are. You might come back again, you know. I might just send them an hour. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Someday we'll try to see your time. Yeah.
We'll have to do a full number now. I wonder if they have...
Let me see the book that you may have... Have you forget it? William Richland.
Well, it's in the book. Full book, too, now. I didn't know it.
R-I-D-G-L-E-Y. Yes.
Well, how is the spelling again?
R-I-D-G-L-E-Y. L-E-Y. Yes. It's the English line.
Well, somebody spelled it wrong once, and I didn't know just how to spell it for sure. I heard that E go. Yeah.

E. Something used to me, but not that. Then I was a self-made man. When my mother died, I was promoted to second grade. And school closed. See, I was promoted. When school opened again, I never did get back. So I never did take a lesson in second grade. But this would happen.
You are a way.
